analysis.one_liner: Max Healthcare Institute runs a network of multi-specialty hospitals concentrated in Delhi-NCR and North India, offering tertiary and quaternary care in areas like oncology, cardiac sciences and transplants.
analysis.whats_happening: The stock has fallen to a 52-week low after the Supreme Court, hearing a case on cancer-drug mark-ups, flagged instances of drugs bought by hospitals for roughly ₹2,700 being billed to patients at an MRP of ₹27,000, and floated a 16% margin cap on hospital pharmacy sales. The government has separately expanded a 30% trade-margin cap to more oncology drugs (list widened 8 Oct 2026), with a further Supreme Court hearing on 12 Oct 2026. Q1 FY27 results (13 Aug 2026) already showed oncology under pressure before this escalated. Q2 FY27 results are expected around mid-November 2026 (exact date not yet confirmed), so this isn't an imminent-date situation.
analysis.plain_terms: This is a hospital chain, and on the operating side it looks healthy: more patients, more beds filled, more international patients, and a bolt-on hospital acquisition (Kalinga, in Bhubaneswar) adding to revenue. The tension is that courts and the government are now scrutinising what hospitals charge for cancer drugs through their in-house pharmacies, which is a real profit pool for a chain like this. The market has reacted as if that profit pool could shrink, and because the stock was priced at a rich valuation for a hospital business, even a modest threat to margins has hit the price hard.
analysis.quarters: Q1 FY27 (Jun 2026, reported 13 Aug 2026): network gross revenue ₹2,982 Cr (+16% YoY), network EBITDA ₹704 Cr (+15% YoY) at a near-flat 24.8% margin (vs 24.9%), network PAT ₹357 Cr vs ₹345 Cr (+~3-5%, slower than revenue, consistent with oncology pressure). On a strictly consolidated basis (Screener), PAT was ₹323 Cr vs ₹308 Cr a year earlier. International patient revenue grew 18% to ₹247 Cr (9% of hospital revenue). Note: Max reports a larger 'network' revenue figure that includes hospitals run under O&M contracts but not fully consolidated — not directly comparable to the smaller reported consolidated revenue line, so don't mix the two series. Also flag: Q2 FY26 (Sep 2025) consolidated PAT spiked to ₹491 Cr partly because of a one-off ₹149 Cr favourable tax impact from a subsidiary merger (CRL-JHL) — management itself said underlying PAT growth that quarter was 16%, not the 59-74% headline jump reported in some sources off a distorted base.
analysis.performance_read: There is no split, bonus or demerger in the data (has_corporate_action is false), so the drawdown is a genuine price fall, not a corporate-action artifact. The stock is down 33.9% from its July 2025 peak and sits at a 52-week low, underperforming both the Nifty and peer Apollo Hospitals sharply over 3 months (-21.9% vs -4.5% and -11.1%) and over 1 year (-25.6% vs -9.2% and +1.1%). That is unusual — it points to a company/sector-specific regulatory scare rather than a broad market move. Zoom out and the picture flips: over 3 years the stock is up 49.5% (vs Nifty 16.6%, though behind peer's 58.3%), and over 5 years it is up a striking 149.6% against Nifty's 24.5% and peer's 84.7%. So long-term holders are still comfortably ahead; it is the most recent year that has been painful.
analysis.valuation_read: At a P/E near 55x and P/B near 7.7x, this is an expensive stock in absolute terms. It looks relatively less stretched only because hospital-sector peers trade even richer (peer median P/E cited around 60-63x) — that is a sector-wide premium, not evidence the stock itself is cheap. ROCE of about 14.7-15% is slightly below the sector peer median (~15.9%), so the returns on capital don't obviously justify the multiple; the market has been paying up for growth expectations that the current regulatory scrutiny now puts a question mark over.
analysis.growth_read: Revenue grew about 16% YoY in the latest quarter, but part of that is inorganic — the Kalinga Hospital (Bhubaneswar) and Yerawada Properties (Pune) acquisitions added to the topline, not just existing hospitals doing more business. On the organic side, occupied-bed-days grew 10% YoY with occupancy at 75% and EBITDA margin flat at 24.8%, so the organic growth that is happening is volume-led (more patients, more beds filled) rather than margin-led. Oncology, specifically, is now a drag rather than a driver because of discontinued high-markup drugs and price-cap risk.
analysis.health_read: Financial risk looks low: borrowings of about ₹3,478 Cr against a ₹17,184 Cr asset base put debt-to-equity around 0.32-0.36x, and debt-to-EBITDA around 1.5x — manageable leverage, and profits have historically converted into reported cash earnings without obvious red flags in the data gathered here. The real risk sitting over this stock is business/regulatory risk, not balance-sheet risk: a potential structural cut to pharmacy margins on cancer (and possibly other) drugs. One sector note estimated roughly a 5% hit to EBITDA from the oncology margin cap specifically — flagging this as an estimate from a single broker source, not verified independently.
analysis.ownership_read: Promoter Abhay Soi holds about 23.71% of the company (with Aditya Soi as promoter group), and the promoters formally declared zero share pledge/encumbrance for FY26 (filed with exchanges on 6 April 2026) — a clean signal on that front. Institutional ownership is heavy: FII/FPI holding was around 45.4% and DII around 26.3% as of the March 2026 quarter. No widely known individual marquee investor was found on the shareholding register in the sources checked — not verified either way, so nothing should be assumed on that score.
strengths: Network revenue grew 16% YoY to ₹2,982 Cr in Q1 FY27 with international patient revenue up 18% to ₹247 Cr (9% of hospital revenue)
Low financial leverage: debt-to-equity around 0.32-0.36x and debt-to-EBITDA near 1.5x
Promoters declared zero pledged shares for FY26, filed 6 April 2026
Strong long-run track record: stock up 149.6% over 5 years versus Nifty's 24.5%, despite the recent fall
watchpoints: Supreme Court hearing (12 Oct 2026) and government trade-margin caps on cancer drugs (30% cap, with the Court floating 16%) — one broker estimate puts the EBITDA hit at roughly 5%, not yet confirmed in reported numbers
Stock is at a 52-week low, down 33.9% from its July 2025 peak and underperforming Nifty and peer Apollo badly over both 3 months and 1 year
Valuation still rich at ~55x P/E and ~7.7x P/B even after the fall, with ROCE (14.7%) trailing the peer median (~15.9%)
A meaningful share of recent revenue growth is inorganic (Kalinga and Yerawada stakes), so headline growth overstates organic momentum
analysis.one_thing: The scope and level of the final trade-margin cap on cancer (and potentially other) drugs that emerges from the Supreme Court process and government notifications — that determines whether the EBITDA hit stays near the ~5% estimate already circulating or turns out larger, and whether oncology economics change structurally for the hospital sector.
analysis.data_notes: Q1 FY27 revenue/EBITDA/PAT cross-checked across Kotak, Investywise and Screener.in; flagged a real non-comparability issue between Max's self-reported 'network' figures (include non-consolidated O&M hospitals) and Screener's consolidated reported financials — used consolidated as the default series. The Q2 FY26 (Sep 2025) PAT spike was traced to a one-off ₹149 Cr merger-related tax benefit, management's own disclosed figure, and excluded from the underlying growth read. Could not verify an exact Q2 FY27 results date (expected mid-November 2026 based on the prior-year pattern, unconfirmed) or confirm/deny any marquee individual investor on the shareholding register — both marked not verified rather than guessed.
